claim: An S3 origin configured as a website endpoint is considered a custom origin, and when you create the distribution through the API you must configure it with CustomOriginConfig.
question: Is an S3 bucket that is configured as a website endpoint a custom origin in CloudFront?

values.display: also considered a custom origin
you must configure it by using CustomOriginConfig

evidence.quote: An Amazon S3 origin configured as a website endpoint is also considered a custom origin.

If you use the CloudFront API to create your distribution with an Amazon S3 bucket that is configured as a website endpoint, you must configure it by using `CustomOriginConfig`, even though the website is hosted in an Amazon S3 bucket.

claim: Private content is the exception among the CloudFront features for custom origins: a signed URL can be used, but for CloudFront to reach a custom origin the origin must stay publicly accessible.

the origin must remain publicly accessible

evidence.quote: Most CloudFront features are supported when you use a custom origin with the exception of private content. Although you can use a signed URL to distribute content from a custom origin, for CloudFront to access the custom origin, the origin must remain publicly accessible.

claim: If a distribution has additional cache behaviors, the default cache behavior is always the last one processed; the others are processed in the order in which they are listed.

Other cache behaviors are processed in the order in which they're listed in the CloudFront console or, if you're using the CloudFront API, the order in which they're listed in the `DistributionConfig` element for the distribution.

claim: CloudFront compares the requested path with the path patterns in the order in which the cache behaviors are listed, and the first match decides which cache behavior applies.

compared with path patterns in the order

evidence.quote: When CloudFront receives an end-user request, the requested path is compared with path patterns in the order in which cache behaviors are listed in the distribution. The first match determines which cache behavior is applied to that request.

claim: Each cache behavior names exactly one origin, so a distribution needs at least as many cache behaviors (the default one included) as it has origins to use all of them.

at least as many cache behaviors

evidence.quote: When you create a cache behavior, you specify the one origin from which you want CloudFront to get objects. As a result, if you want CloudFront to distribute objects from all of your origins, you must have at least as many cache behaviors (including the default cache behavior) as you have origins.

claim: CloudFront caches responses to GET and HEAD requests and, optionally, OPTIONS requests; it does not cache responses to requests that use other methods.
question: Which HTTP method responses does CloudFront cache?

values.display: caches responses to GET and HEAD requests
does not cache responses to requests that use other methods

evidence.quote: CloudFront caches responses to `GET` and `HEAD` requests and, optionally, `OPTIONS` requests. Responses to `OPTIONS` requests are cached separately from responses to `GET` and `HEAD` requests (the `OPTIONS` method is included in the [cache key](understanding-the-cache-key.md) for `OPTIONS` requests). CloudFront does not cache responses to requests that use other methods.

claim: For gRPC, the allowed HTTP methods must be GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, POST, PATCH, DELETE, because gRPC workloads require the POST method.

evidence.quote: If you're using gRPC in your workload, you must select **GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, POST, PATCH, DELETE**. gRPC workloads require the `POST` method.
